claim: In most of the world, mammography screening programmes were paused at the start of the pandemic.
source: In most of the world, the mammography screening programmes were paused at the start of the pandemic, whilst mammography screening continued in Denmark.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by multiple citations in the introduction section discussing temporary closures in other countries.

claim: Mammography screening continued in Denmark during the COVID-19 pandemic.
source: In most of the world, the mammography screening programmes were paused at the start of the pandemic, whilst mammography screening continued in Denmark.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract and elaborated throughout the manuscript as the unique context of the study.

claim: The study population comprised 1,828,791 invitations among 847,766 women aged 50-69 years invited to participate in mammography screening from 2016 to 2021 in Denmark.
source: The study population comprised all women aged 50–69 years old invited to participate in mammography screening from 2016 to 2021 in Denmark based on data from the Danish Quality Database for Mammography Screening in combination with population-based registries.
evidence: The study population is explicitly described in the abstract and methods, with specific numbers provided in the results section.

claim: Before the pandemic, 80.2% of invitations resulted in participation in mammography screening within 90 days.
source: Before the pandemic, 80.2% of invitations resulted in participation in mammography screening within 90 d, 82.7% within 180 d, and 83.1% within 365 d.
evidence: This is a direct data finding stated in the abstract and results section.

claim: Before the pandemic, 82.7% of invitations resulted in participation in mammography screening within 180 days.
source: Before the pandemic, 80.2% of invitations resulted in participation in mammography screening within 90 d, 82.7% within 180 d, and 83.1% within 365 d.
evidence: This is a direct data finding stated in the abstract and results section.

claim: Before the pandemic, 83.1% of invitations resulted in participation in mammography screening within 365 days.
source: Before the pandemic, 80.2% of invitations resulted in participation in mammography screening within 90 d, 82.7% within 180 d, and 83.1% within 365 d.
evidence: This is a direct data finding stated in the abstract and results section.

claim: At the start of the pandemic, participation in screening within 90 days was reduced to 69.9% for those invited in pre-lockdown.
source: At the start of the pandemic, the participation in screening within 90 d was reduced to 69.9% for those invited in pre-lockdown and to 76.5% for those invited in first lockdown.
evidence: This is a direct data finding stated in the abstract.

claim: At the start of the pandemic, participation in screening within 90 days was reduced to 76.5% for those invited in first lockdown.
source: At the start of the pandemic, the participation in screening within 90 d was reduced to 69.9% for those invited in pre-lockdown and to 76.5% for those invited in first lockdown.
evidence: This is a direct data finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Extending the follow-up time to 365 days, only a minor overall reduction in participation was observed (PR = 0.94; 95% CI: 0.93–0.95 in pre-lockdown).
source: Extending the length of follow-up time to 365 d only a minor overall reduction was observed (PR = 0.94; 95% CI: 0.93–0.95 in pre-lockdown and PR = 0.97; 95% CI: 0.96–0.97 in first lockdown).
evidence: This is a direct statistical finding with prevalence ratios and confidence intervals provided.

claim: Extending the follow-up time to 365 days, only a minor overall reduction in participation was observed (PR = 0.97; 95% CI: 0.96–0.97 in first lockdown).
source: Extending the length of follow-up time to 365 d only a minor overall reduction was observed (PR = 0.94; 95% CI: 0.93–0.95 in pre-lockdown and PR = 0.97; 95% CI: 0.96–0.97 in first lockdown).
evidence: This is a direct statistical finding with prevalence ratios and confidence intervals provided.

claim: Lower participation was observed among immigrants during the pandemic.
source: A lower participation was, however, seen among immigrants and among women with a low income.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by detailed data in the results section.

claim: Lower participation was observed among women with a low income during the pandemic.
source: A lower participation was, however, seen among immigrants and among women with a low income.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by detailed data in the results section.

claim: The social inequity in screening participation was exacerbated during the pandemic.
source: Some groups of women, nonetheless, had a lower participation, indicating that the social inequity in screening participation was exacerbated during the pandemic.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data findings regarding differential participation rates among socioeconomic groups.

claim: The study was funded by the Danish Cancer Society Scientific Committee (grant number R321-A17417) and the Danish regions.
source: The study was funded by the Danish Cancer Society Scientific Committee (grant number R321-A17417) and the Danish regions.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract.

claim: Population-wide restrictions ('lockdowns') were imposed worldwide to minimise the spread of infection with COVID-19.
source: Population-wide restrictions ('lockdowns') were imposed worldwide to minimise the spread of infection with COVID-19 and to lessen the burden on the healthcare systems.
evidence: This is a statement of general knowledge about the pandemic response.

claim: The European Society for Medical Oncology deemed population-based mammography screening to be of low priority at the start of the pandemic.
source: Congruently, the European Society for Medical Oncology deemed population-based mammography screening to be of low priority at the start of the pandemic (de Azambuja et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to de Azambuja et al., 2020.

claim: In Denmark, early detection of cancer was considered of high priority during the pandemic.
source: Nevertheless, in Denmark the mammography screening programme continued – and invitations and reminders were sent out – throughout the pandemic since early detection of cancer was considered of high priority.
evidence: This is stated as the rationale for continuing screening in Denmark.

claim: Studies from other countries have shown marked reductions in breast cancer screening during the pandemic as a result of temporary closures of screening programmes.
source: Studies from other countries have shown marked reductions in breast cancer screening during the pandemic as a result of the temporary closures of the screening programmes (Ng and Hamilton, 2022; Cairns et al., 2022; Jidkova et al., 2022; Miller et al., 2021; Sprague et al., 2021); however, the participation in mammography screening in Denmark with a continuation of the programme has not yet been described.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies from other countries.

claim: Disruptions to the mammography screening programme could result in later diagnosis of breast cancer and a more advanced stage of diagnosis.
source: Disruptions to the mammography screening programme could result in later diagnosis of breast cancer and a more advanced stage of diagnosis (Figueroa et al., 2021), and the disruptions to the programme are therefore worrisome.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Figueroa et al., 2021.

claim: Studies from the Netherlands found that the temporary closure of the screening programme resulted in a reduction in the number of breast cancer diagnoses, in particular screen-detected breast cancers.
source: Congruently, studies from the Netherlands found that the temporary closure of the screening programme resulted in a reduction in the number of breast cancer diagnoses, in particular screen-detected breast cancers (Eijkelboom et al., 2021b; Dinmohamed et al., 2020) and in particular among early-stage tumours (Eijkelboom et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies from the Netherlands.

claim: An early study reported that a 19% reduction in the number of breast cancers was observed in Denmark in the spring of 2020.
source: In Denmark, an early study reported that a 19% reduction in the number of breast cancers was observed in the spring of 2020 (Skovlund et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Skovlund et al., 2022.

claim: More recent data from the Danish Breast Cancer Group show a modest reduction of 5% in the number of breast cancer in 2020 compared to 2019.
source: Contrarily, more recent data from the Danish Breast Cancer Group show a modest reduction of 5% in the number of breast cancer in 2020 compared to 2019 (The Danish Clinical Quality Program – National Clinical Registries, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to The Danish Clinical Quality Program – National Clinical Registries, 2022.

claim: The participation in mammography screening is generally lower among women with low socio-economic status.
source: The participation in mammography screening is generally lower among women with low socio-economic status and among immigrant women (Bhargava et al., 2018; Kristiansen et al., 2012; Jensen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The participation in mammography screening is generally lower among immigrant women.
source: The participation in mammography screening is generally lower among women with low socio-economic status and among immigrant women (Bhargava et al., 2018; Kristiansen et al., 2012; Jensen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: One study from Spain found that the participation in mammography screening decreased with age and with lower socio-economic level post-COVID-19.
source: One study from Spain Bosch et al., 2022 found that the participation in mammography screening decreased with age and with lower socio-economic level post-COVID-19; however, to our knowledge, no studies have examined participation according to ethnicity, cohabitation status, or healthcare use throughout the pandemic.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bosch et al., 2022.

claim: Denmark has a population of approximately 5.8 million inhabitants.
source: The study is set in Denmark, which has a population of approximately 5.8 million inhabitants (Statistics Denmark, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Statistics Denmark, 2021.

claim: In Denmark, there is free access to healthcare for all inhabitants funded via taxes.
source: In Denmark, there is free access to healthcare for all inhabitants funded via taxes.
evidence: This is a statement about the Danish healthcare system.

claim: Danish population-based administrative and health registries can be linked using the unique personal identifier assigned to all residents at birth or immigration.
source: Danish population-based administrative and health registries can be linked using the unique personal identifier, assigned to all residents at birth or immigration (Schmidt et al., 2014; Schmidt et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schmidt et al., 2014 and Schmidt et al., 2019.

claim: In Denmark, all women aged 50-69 years old are invited to participate in mammography screening every 2 years.
source: In Denmark, all women aged 50-69 years old are invited to participate in mammography screening every 2 y (except women, who have opted out of the programme).
evidence: This describes the Danish mammography screening programme.

claim: The mammography screening programme is administered by the five Danish regions.
source: The mammography screening programme is administered by the five Danish regions.
evidence: This describes the administrative structure of the screening programme.

claim: Digital invitation letters with a fixed appointment and link to an information leaflet are sent to women for mammography screening in Denmark.
source: Digital invitation letters with a fixed appointment and link to an information leaflet are sent to the women.
evidence: This describes the invitation process for the screening programme.

claim: At the mammography screening session, two standardised X-ray images of each breast are performed and evaluated independently by two radiologists.
source: At the mammography screening session, two standardised X-ray images of each breast are performed and these images are evaluated independently by two radiologists (Mikkelsen et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the screening procedure and is supported by a citation to Mikkelsen et al., 2016.

claim: Three main waves of the COVID-19 pandemic have occurred in Denmark: in the spring of 2020, in the winter of 2020/2021, and again in the winter of 2021/2022.
source: Three main waves of the COVID-19 pandemic have occurred in Denmark, that is, in the spring of 2020, in the winter of 2020/2021, and again in the winter of 2021/2022 (Statens Serum Institut, 2021a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Statens Serum Institut, 2021a.

claim: The first lockdown was imposed in Denmark on 11 March 2020.
source: The first lockdown was imposed in Denmark on 11 March 2020, closing down schools and workplaces and restricting travel.
evidence: This is a statement of fact about the pandemic response in Denmark.

claim: Widespread COVID-19 testing was implemented in Denmark from May 2020 providing PCR and antigen COVID-19 tests free of charge to the whole population.
source: Widespread COVID-19 testing was implemented in Denmark from May 2020 providing PCR and antigen COVID-19 tests free of charge to the whole population (Pottegård et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pottegård et al., 2020.

claim: Vaccination against COVID-19 was implemented in Denmark in December 2020.
source: Vaccination against COVID-19 was implemented in Denmark in December 2020, and by March 2022, approximately 81% of the population had received two doses and more than 61% had received three doses of the vaccine (Statens Serum Institut, 2021b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Statens Serum Institut, 2021b.

claim: By March 2022, approximately 81% of the Danish population had received two doses of COVID-19 vaccine.
source: Vaccination against COVID-19 was implemented in Denmark in December 2020, and by March 2022, approximately 81% of the population had received two doses and more than 61% had received three doses of the vaccine (Statens Serum Institut, 2021b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Statens Serum Institut, 2021b.

claim: By March 2022, more than 61% of the Danish population had received three doses of COVID-19 vaccine.
source: Vaccination against COVID-19 was implemented in Denmark in December 2020, and by March 2022, approximately 81% of the population had received two doses and more than 61% had received three doses of the vaccine (Statens Serum Institut, 2021b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Statens Serum Institut, 2021b.

claim: The study included all invitations to women aged 50–69 years invited to participate in mammography screening from 1 January 2016 to 30 September 2021 as registered in the Danish Quality Database for Mammography Screening.
source: We included all invitations to women aged 50–69 y invited to participate in mammography screening from 1 January 2016 to 30 September 2021 as registered in the Danish Quality Database for Mammography Screening (Mikkelsen et al., 2016), which retrieves information on invitations to the national mammography screening programme directly from the regional administrative systems.
evidence: This describes the study population and data source.

claim: Invitations to women with an unknown postal address (N = 753 in 406 women) were excluded from the study.
source: We excluded invitations to women with an unknown postal address (N = 753 in 406 women), invitations to women residing in the Faroe Islands or Greenland (N = 310 in 220 women), invitations to women with unknown/uncertain living status (N = 199 in 146 women), invitations to women who emigrated within 1 y since invitation (N = 2692 in 2,581 women), invitations to women who died within 1 y since invitation (N = 8860 in 8,854 women), and women excluded due to dates being out of order (e.g. pre-booked date for mammography screening was prior to date of invitation; N = 8218 in 1,023 women) (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes exclusion criteria and is shown in Figure 1.

source: We excluded invitations to women with an unknown postal address (N = 753 in 406 women), invitations to women residing in the Faroe Islands or Greenland (N = 310 in 220 women), invitations to women with unknown/uncertain living status (N = 199 in 146 women), invitations to women who emigrated within 1 y since invitation (N = 2692 in 2,581 women), invitations to women who died within 1 y since invitation (N = 8860 in 8,854 women), and women excluded due to dates being out of order (e.g. pre-booked date for mammography screening was prior to date of invitation; N = 8218 in 1,023 women) (Figure 1).

claim: The majority of women in the study were of Danish descent (91.7%).
source: The majority were of Danish descent (91.7%), the median age was 58 years old (interdecentile interval [IQI] = 54–64), most were married (60.2%), and the majority had a short educational level (58.7%).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the study population.

claim: The median age of women in the study was 58 years old (interdecentile interval [IQI] = 54–64).
source: The majority were of Danish descent (91.7%), the median age was 58 years old (interdecentile interval [IQI] = 54–64), most were married (60.2%), and the majority had a short educational level (58.7%).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the study population.

claim: Most women in the study were married (60.2%).
source: The majority were of Danish descent (91.7%), the median age was 58 years old (interdecentile interval [IQI] = 54–64), most were married (60.2%), and the majority had a short educational level (58.7%).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the study population.

claim: The majority of women in the study had a short educational level (58.7%).

evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the study population.

claim: At the start of the pandemic, a reduction of 3.7–10.6 percentage points in screening participation within 90 days was observed.
source: At the start of the pandemic, a reduction of 3.7–10.6 percentage points in screening participation within 90 d was observed (PR = 0.85; 95% CI: 084–0.85 in pre-lockdown and PR = 0.93; 95% CI: 0.92–0.94 in first lockdown) corresponding to a participation rate of 69.6% among women invited during pre-lockdown and 76.5% among women invited during the first lockdown, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct data finding with statistical measures provided.

claim: The participation rate within 90 days was 69.6% among women invited during pre-lockdown.
source: At the start of the pandemic, a reduction of 3.7–10.6 percentage points in screening participation within 90 d was observed (PR = 0.85; 95% CI: 084–0.85 in pre-lockdown and PR = 0.93; 95% CI: 0.92–0.94 in first lockdown) corresponding to a participation rate of 69.6% among women invited during pre-lockdown and 76.5% among women invited during the first lockdown, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct data finding.

claim: The participation in mammography screening within 365 days was reduced by 1.6–3.5 percentage points at the start of the pandemic.
source: The participation in mammography screening within 365 d was also reduced by 1.6–3.5 percentage points (PR = 0.94; 95% CI: 0.93–0.95 among women invited during pre-lockdown and PR = 0.97; 95% CI: 0.96–0.97 among women invited during the first lockdown) corresponding to a participation rate of 79.6% during pre-lockdown and 81.5% during the first lockdown.
evidence: This is a direct data finding with statistical measures provided.

claim: The participation rate within 365 days was 79.6% during pre-lockdown.
source: The participation in mammography screening within 365 d was also reduced by 1.6–3.5 percentage points (PR = 0.94; 95% CI: 0.93–0.95 among women invited during pre-lockdown and PR = 0.97; 95% CI: 0.96–0.97 among women invited during the first lockdown) corresponding to a participation rate of 79.6% during pre-lockdown and 81.5% during the first lockdown.
evidence: This is a direct data finding.

claim: The participation rate within 365 days was 81.5% during the first lockdown.
source: The participation in mammography screening within 365 d was also reduced by 1.6–3.5 percentage points (PR = 0.94; 95% CI: 0.93–0.95 among women invited during pre-lockdown and PR = 0.97; 95% CI: 0.96–0.97 among women invited during the first lockdown) corresponding to a participation rate of 79.6% during pre-lockdown and 81.5% during the first lockdown.
evidence: This is a direct data finding.

claim: The overall participation resumed to pre-pandemic levels from first reopening and onwards.
source: Again, the overall participation resumed to pre-pandemic levels from first reopening and onwards (Table 2 and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Table 2.

claim: Before the pandemic, the participation in mammography screening within 90 days was lowest among the youngest women (77.6%).
source: Before the pandemic, the participation in mammography screening within 90 and 365 d was the lowest among the youngest women (77.6 and 80.9%), among immigrants (67.8 and 70.7% among Western and 66.8 and 69.9% among non-Western immigrants), among women living alone (72.1 and 75.2%), among women with the lowest income (73.8 and 76.1%), and among women who rarely use the primary healthcare system (75.4 and 78.2%) (Supplementary files 1-3).
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the data.

claim: Before the pandemic, the participation in mammography screening within 90 days was 67.8% among Western immigrants.
source: Before the pandemic, the participation in mammography screening within 90 and 365 d was the lowest among the youngest women (77.6 and 80.9%), among immigrants (67.8 and 70.7% among Western and 66.8 and 69.9% among non-Western immigrants), among women living alone (72.1 and 75.2%), among women with the lowest income (73.8 and 76.1%), and among women who rarely use the primary healthcare system (75.4 and 78.2%) (Supplementary files 1-3).

claim: The reduction in participation within 90 days at the start of the pandemic was most pronounced in the oldest age group (to 70.3% in pre-lockdown and 76.6% in first lockdown).
source: The reduction in participation within 90 d at the start of the pandemic was most pronounced in the oldest age group (to 70.3% in pre-lockdown and 76.6% in first lockdown), among immigrants (to 55.1% among Western and 53.2% among non-Western immigrants in pre-lockdown), among women with a low income (to 60.1% in pre-lockdown and 66.7% in first lockdown), and women who frequently use the primary healthcare system (to 68.6% in pre-lockdown).
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the data analysis.

claim: The reduction in participation within 90 days at the start of the pandemic was most pronounced among Western immigrants (to 55.1% in pre-lockdown).

source: Extending the length of follow-up time to 365 d, a lower participation remained among immigrants (65.6% among Western and 64.2% among non-Western immigrants in pre-lockdown) and among women with a low income (69.3% in pre-lockdown and 71.5% in first lockdown) for those invited at the start of the pandemic.

claim: The reduced participation was observed throughout the study period among women with a low income.
source: The reduced participation was observed throughout the study period among women with a low income (Table 2 and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Table 2.

claim: The short-term reduction in mammography screening participation may have been caused by the governmental instructions to stay at home.
source: We found a short-term reduction in participation in mammography screening at the start of the pandemic, which may have been caused by the governmental instructions to stay at home.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: A qualitative study from Denmark found that women weighed the benefits of screening versus the risk of acquiring COVID-19 in their decision-making process as to whether to participate in mammography screening during the pandemic.
source: Congruently, a qualitative study from Denmark found that women weighed the benefits of screening versus the risk of acquiring COVID-19 in their decision-making process as to whether to participate in mammography screening during the pandemic (Kirkegaard et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kirkegaard et al., 2021.

claim: COVID-19 vaccination implementation in Denmark in December 2020 could explain the unaltered participation in mammography screening during the second reopening of the society.
source: COVID-19 vaccination was implemented in Denmark in December 2020, which could explain the unaltered participation in mammography screening during the second reopening of the society.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: During the pandemic, initiatives were made throughout Denmark to inform women of the possibility of participating in mammography screening during the pandemic and to inform women about safety measures when participating in screening.
source: During the pandemic, initiatives were made throughout Denmark to inform women of the possibility of participating in mammography screening during the pandemic and to inform women about safety measures when participating in screening; for example, a letter was sent to women opting out of the programme (i.e. withdrawing from the screening programme) in some regions, in some regions press releases were sent out and in some regions, and women calling in to cancel their appointment for mammography screening were individually counselled and encouraged to consider participation later on (instead of waiting for the next biannual round of screening).
evidence: This describes interventions implemented during the pandemic.

claim: The participation dropped by 3.3% among women of Danish descent for those invited during pre-lockdown.
source: The participation dropped by 3.3% among women of Danish descent for those invited during pre-lockdown, whilst the participation dropped by 5.0% among Western and 5.7% among non-Western immigrants.
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the data analysis.

claim: The participation dropped by 5.0% among Western immigrants for those invited during pre-lockdown.
source: The participation dropped by 3.3% among women of Danish descent for those invited during pre-lockdown, whilst the participation dropped by 5.0% among Western and 5.7% among non-Western immigrants.
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the data analysis.

claim: The participation dropped by 5.7% among non-Western immigrants for those invited during pre-lockdown.
source: The participation dropped by 3.3% among women of Danish descent for those invited during pre-lockdown, whilst the participation dropped by 5.0% among Western and 5.7% among non-Western immigrants.
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the data analysis.

claim: Among women with the lowest income, the participation dropped by 6.9% during pre-lockdown.
source: Even larger differences were seen when stratifying by income level: among women with the lowest income, the participation dropped by 6.9% during pre-lockdown and by 4.6% during the first lockdown, whilst the participation among women with the highest income was almost unchanged.
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the data analysis.

claim: Among women with the lowest income, the participation dropped by 4.6% during the first lockdown.
source: Even larger differences were seen when stratifying by income level: among women with the lowest income, the participation dropped by 6.9% during pre-lockdown and by 4.6% during the first lockdown, whilst the participation among women with the highest income was almost unchanged.
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the data analysis.

claim: The participation among women with the highest income was almost unchanged during the pandemic.
source: Even larger differences were seen when stratifying by income level: among women with the lowest income, the participation dropped by 6.9% during pre-lockdown and by 4.6% during the first lockdown, whilst the participation among women with the highest income was almost unchanged.
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the data analysis.

claim: The restrictions imposed in Denmark may have affected some groups of women disproportionally.
source: This indicates that the restrictions imposed in Denmark may have affected some groups of women disproportionally.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the differential participation rates observed.

claim: The COVID-19 vaccination coverage was lower among immigrants.
source: Moreover, the COVID-19 vaccination coverage was lower among immigrants (Gram et al., 2023), which could partly explain the lower screening participation.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gram et al., 2023.

claim: Women with a low income may not have access to private means of transport and may have been reluctant to use public transportation to reach a mammography screening clinic during the pandemic.
source: Women with a low income may not have access to private means of transport and may have been reluctant to use public transportation to reach a mammography screening clinic during the pandemic, which could explain the lower participation among this group of women.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed lower participation.

claim: Women without private means of transport generally have a lower participation in mammography screening.
source: Women without private means of transport generally have a lower participation in mammography screening (Jensen et al., 2012; Jensen et al., 2014), and this may have worsened during the pandemic.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jensen et al., 2012 and Jensen et al., 2014.

claim: The lower participation in screening continued throughout the study period among women with a low income, indicating that the pandemic had lasting negative effects on the participation in mammography screening in this group of women.
source: The lower participation in screening continued throughout the study period among women with a low income, indicating that the pandemic had lasting negative effects on the participation in mammography screening in this group of women.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the persistent lower participation observed in the data.

claim: Danish administrative and health registries have a high completeness.
source: Danish administrative and health registries have a high completeness (Thygesen et al., 2011), which is also the case for the Danish Quality Database for Mammography Screening (Mikkelsen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Thygesen et al., 2011 and Mikkelsen et al., 2016.

claim: The Danish Quality Database for Mammography Screening has high completeness.
source: Danish administrative and health registries have a high completeness (Thygesen et al., 2011), which is also the case for the Danish Quality Database for Mammography Screening (Mikkelsen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mikkelsen et al., 2016.

claim: Denmark managed to keep the number of hospitalisations due to COVID-19 at a relatively low level.
source: Moreover, the severity of the pandemic and the pandemic response was different in different countries, with Denmark managing to keep the number of hospitalisations due to COVID-19 at a relatively low level (Statens Serum Institut, 2021a), and our observations may not be directly transferable to all countries.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Statens Serum Institut, 2021a.

claim: Women postponed screening at the start of the pandemic.
source: Our study indicates that women postponed screening at the start of the pandemic.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data showing short-term reduction but longer-term recovery in participation.

claim: Inconsistent health messages may have resulted in a reduced participation in screening.
source: Inconsistent health messages may thus have resulted in a reduced participation in screening.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: The effect of the short-term reduction in mammography screening participation on the detection of early-stage breast cancer is unknown.
source: The effect of the short-term reduction in mammography screening participation on the detection of early-stage breast cancer is unknown.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation in understanding the clinical impact of the findings.

claim: Cancer diagnoses have been shown to be incompletely registered for months.
source: A study from Denmark by Skovlund et al., 2022 reported a 19% reduction in breast cancers diagnosed in the spring of 2020; however, this large reduction may partly be a result of a delayed registration of cancer diagnoses at the time of that study as cancer diagnoses have been shown to be incompletely registered for months (Larsen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Larsen et al., 2014.

claim: The lower participation at the start of the pandemic most likely only has a minor effect on the overall mortality from breast cancer at a population level.
source: However, since by far most women merely postponed their participation and showed up later, the lower participation at the start of the pandemic most likely only has a minor effect on the overall mortality from breast cancer at a population level.
evidence: This is an interpretation and speculation based on the finding that most women eventually participated.

claim: The short-term mammography screening participation was reduced at the start of the pandemic.
source: We found that the short-term mammography screening participation was reduced at the start of the pandemic, whilst only a minor reduction in participation was observed with longer follow-up time.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Only a minor reduction in participation was observed with longer follow-up time.
source: We found that the short-term mammography screening participation was reduced at the start of the pandemic, whilst only a minor reduction in participation was observed with longer follow-up time.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Some groups of women (immigrants and women with a low income) had a lower participation even with the longest follow-up time.
source: Some groups of women (immigrants and women with a low income) had a lower participation even with the longest follow-up time, indicating that the social inequity in mammography screening participation was slightly exacerbated during the pandemic.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: The social inequity in mammography screening participation was slightly exacerbated during the pandemic.
source: Some groups of women (immigrants and women with a low income) had a lower participation even with the longest follow-up time, indicating that the social inequity in mammography screening participation was slightly exacerbated during the pandemic.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the differential participation rates observed.
